title: Present Rates of Contribution (EPF, EPS, EDLI and Administrative/Inspection charges)
applicability: All establishments covered under the EPF & MP Act, 1952 and their employees. Governs monthly statutory payroll deductions and employer liability. Directly relevant for computing PF on payroll: the 12%/10% rate, the Rs.15,000 wage ceiling, the 8.33% EPS diversion, EDLI 0.5%, and EPF admin charges 0.50% (min Rs.500).
seedText: PRESENT RATES OF CONTRIBUTION. Employee EPF share: 12% (or 10% in specified cases); Employee EPS/EDLI: nil. Employer: EPF = difference of employee share and pension contribution; EPS (A/C 10) = 8.33%; EDLI (A/C 21) = 0.50%. EPF Administrative charges (A/C 2) = 0.50% w.e.f. 01-06-2018, minimum Rs.500/- per month per establishment (Rs.75/- if no contributory member); EDLI administrative charges = 0 w.e.f. 01-04-2017. The 10% rate applies to: any establishment employing less than 20 persons; a sick industrial company declared by BIFR; an establishment whose accumulated losses at year-end equal or exceed its entire net worth; and Jute, Beedi, Brick, Coir and Guar gum factories. UNDER EPF: contributions are payable on a maximum wage ceiling of Rs.15,000/-. An employee may pay at a higher rate but the employer is not obliged to match it; contribution on wages above Rs.15,000 requires a joint request under Para 26(6) of the EPF Scheme and the employer then pays admin charges on the higher wages. For an International Worker the Rs.15,000 wage ceiling is not applicable. UNDER EPS: pension contribution (8.33%) is paid out of the employer's share; not payable once an employee crosses 58 years. UNDER EDLI: contribution paid up to maximum wage ceiling of Rs.15,000 even if PF is paid on higher wages (e.g. Rs.75 for wages above Rs.15,000), rounded to nearest rupee. If exempted under PF Scheme, inspection charges @0.18% (min Rs.5) apply in place of admin charges; if exempted under EDLI, @0.005% (min Re.1). PF contribution rate history: 22.09.1997 onwards 10% with enhanced rate 12%.

title: ITR-4 (Sugam) FAQ — Presumptive Taxation under Sections 44AD/44ADA/44AE and eligibility
applicability: Resident Individuals, HUFs and Firms (other than LLP) with total income up to Rs. 50 lakh who compute business/professional income on a presumptive basis under sections 44AD, 44ADA or 44AE. seedText: ITR-4 (Sugam) can be filed by a Resident Individual, HUF or Firm (other than LLP) whose total income during the financial year does not exceed Rs. 50 lakh and who has income from business or profession computed on a presumptive basis under section 44AD, 44ADA or 44AE, in addition to income from salary/pension, one house property, and other sources. Long-term capital gain under section 112A not exceeding Rs. 1.25 lakh is permitted; agricultural income must not exceed Rs. 5,000. Section 44AD (eligible business) allows declaration of income at a presumptive rate with a turnover limit of Rs. 3 crore (where cash receipts do not exceed 5% of total receipts) or otherwise Rs. 2 crore; it excludes agency business and income from commission or brokerage. Section 44ADA (specified professions such as legal, medical, engineering, accountancy, technical consultancy and interior decoration) applies where gross receipts do not exceed Rs. 50 lakh (or Rs. 75 lakh subject to the cash-receipt condition), with presumptive income at 50% of gross receipts. Section 44AE applies to a person owning not more than ten goods carriages. ITR-4 cannot be filed by a person who is RNOR or a Non-Resident, a director in a company, a holder of unlisted equity shares, or a person having short-term capital gains or LTCG exceeding Rs. 1.25 lakh. Under the presumptive schemes no further deduction of business expenses is allowed against the presumed income.

seedText: Form GSTR-9 is an annual return to be filed once, for each financial year, by registered taxpayers who were regular taxpayers, including SEZ units and SEZ developers. Filers furnish details of purchases, sales, input tax credit availed and reversed, refunds claimed, and demands created for the year. To file, navigate on www.gst.gov.in to Services > Returns > Annual Return, select the financial year and click PREPARE ONLINE. From FY 2024-25 onwards the portal first asks whether the taxpayer wishes to file a Nil annual return; 'No' is pre-selected where GSTR-1 and GSTR-3B data has been auto-populated. A Nil annual return can be filed only if, for that FY, the taxpayer has NOT made any outward supply, NOT received any goods/services, has NO other liability to report, has NOT claimed any credit and NOT claimed any refund. The manual guides users to download the system-computed GSTR-9 summary, the GSTR-1 and GSTR-3B summaries and the Table 8A document details before entering data across the data-entry tiles spanning Tables 4 to 18 (outward supplies, ITC details and reversals, tax paid, particulars of previous-FY transactions, demands and refunds, and HSN-wise summary of inward/outward supplies). On the HSN summary, if aggregate turnover in the preceding financial year was up to Rs. 5 crore the HSN drop-down permits 4, 6 or 8-digit codes, while turnover above Rs. 5 crore requires at least 6-digit HSN reporting. After entering details the taxpayer previews the draft (PDF/Excel), computes liabilities, pays any late fee, and files using DSC or EVC. Note: GSTR-9 is an annual return and, once filed, cannot be revised.

Form GSTR-9C can be filed only after the annual return Form GSTR-9 has been filed. Pre-conditions: valid GSTIN and login, GSTR-9 filed for the relevant FY, aggregate turnover exceeding the notified threshold, and accounts audited as prescribed. The statement is structured as Part A (reconciliation) and Part B (certification). Part A comprises: PT II — Reconciliation of turnover declared in the audited annual financial statement with turnover declared in the annual return (Form GSTR-9), covering PT II(5) Reconciliation of Gross Turnover, II(6) Reasons for un-reconciled difference in annual gross turnover, II(7) Reconciliation of Taxable Turnover and II(8) Reasons for un-reconciled difference in taxable turnover; PT III — Reconciliation of Tax Paid, tables III(9) to III(11); PT IV — Reconciliation of Input Tax Credit (ITC), tables IV(12) to IV(16) including IV(14) reconciliation of ITC declared in the annual return with ITC availed on expenses per audited financials; and PT V — Auditor's recommendation on additional liability due to non-reconciliation. title: Manual — Viewing Form GSTR-2B (Auto-drafted ITC Statement)
applicability: Every registered person (recipient) who wishes to view/download their auto-drafted Input Tax Credit statement. GSTR-2B is read-only and is not filed; it is used to determine ITC available and not available for a tax period. Generated from suppliers' GSTR-1/IFF/1A, GSTR-5 and ISD GSTR-6 filings.
seedText: Form GSTR-2B is an auto-drafted Input Tax Credit (ITC) statement generated for every registered person on the basis of information furnished by their suppliers in Form GSTR-1, the Invoice Furnishing Facility (IFF) and Form GSTR-1A, by non-resident suppliers in Form GSTR-5, and by Input Service Distributors in Form GSTR-6. It indicates the availability of input tax credit to the recipient against each document filed by suppliers/ISD. GSTR-2B is a read-only static statement: the taxpayer does not file it and cannot add documents or make changes to it. For a given tax period it is available for viewing and downloading in Excel and/or JSON formats in post-login mode on the GST portal. The statement presents a summary split into ITC Available (credit that may be availed, distinguished from amounts to be net-off/reversed) and ITC Not Available, and includes sections for ITC Reversal and, from 1st October 2024 onwards, ITC Rejected. Cut-off dates considered for generation of Form GSTR-2B for the period can be viewed from an advisory pop-up on the portal, so that documents filed by suppliers up to the cut-off are reflected in that period's GSTR-2B and later-filed documents flow into the subsequent period. Because it is static, the GSTR-2B for a period does not change once generated, which helps recipients reconcile eligible ITC before filing GSTR-3B.

publisher: Institute of Chartered Accountants of India
title: Peer Review Mandate - Roll Out (Revised)
applicability: Practice Units (CA firms) rendering assurance/attestation services. Phased mandatory Peer Review Certificate requirement keyed to the type of entity audited and the number of partners in the firm; a pre-requisite before accepting the specified statutory audit assignments.
seedText: This ICAI Peer Review Board announcement (revised roll-out dated 11 April 2022) sets out mandatory Peer Review of Practice Units in four phases, each requiring a valid Peer Review Certificate before undertaking the specified assurance work. Phase I (effective 1 April 2022): Practice Units auditing entities whose equity or debt securities are listed in India or abroad. Phase II (effective 1 April 2023): Practice Units auditing unlisted public companies with paid-up capital of not less than Rs. 500 crore, or annual turnover of not less than Rs. 1000 crore, or aggregate outstanding loans, debentures and deposits of not less than Rs. 500 crore; and Practice Units rendering attestation services with five or more partners. Phase III (effective 1 April 2024): Practice Units auditing entities that have raised funds from public or banks or financial institutions of over Rs. 50 crore during the period under review; and Practice Units rendering attestation services with four or more partners. Phase IV (as originally rolled out, effective 1 April 2025): Practice Units undertaking audits of branches of Public Sector Banks; and Practice Units rendering attestation services with three or more partners. The document states that where, on the date Peer Review becomes mandatory, a Practice Unit already holds a Peer Review Certificate, it need not again be subjected to Peer Review. (Note: the Phase IV start date was subsequently deferred by the Council through later Peer Review Board announcements.)

publisher: Institute of Chartered Accountants of India
title: Applicability of the Revised Edition of Code of Ethics (2019, 12th Edition)
applicability: All members of ICAI (in practice and in service). Governs professional ethics, independence, fundamental principles and conceptual framework for Chartered Accountants; three-volume structure.
seedText: This ICAI announcement notifies the applicability of the revised (12th) edition of the Code of Ethics, 2019. The revised Code was made effective from 1st July 2020. It is organised in three volumes: Code of Ethics Volume I; Code of Ethics Volume II; and Code of Ethics Volume III (Case Laws Referencer). While the revised Code came into effect from 1 July 2020, the Council decided that the applicability of three specific provisions stood deferred until further notice: (1) Responding to Non-Compliance of Laws and Regulations (NOCLAR) [Sections 260 and 360]; (2) Fees - Relative Size [Paragraphs 410.3 to R410.6]; and (3) Taxation Services to Audit Clients [Subsection 604]. All other provisions of the revised Code became applicable from the 1 July 2020 effective date. The revised Code is aligned with the international ethics framework and adapted to Indian domestic law, and governs the fundamental principles of professional ethics (integrity, objectivity, professional competence and due care, confidentiality and professional behaviour), the conceptual framework approach, and independence requirements for members of ICAI in practice and in service.

publisher: Institute of Chartered Accountants of India
title: Clarification on Tax Audit Assignments - Specified Number (Ceiling of 60)
applicability: Chartered Accountants in practice, whether as an individual or as a partner of a firm, accepting tax audit assignments under Section 44AB of the Income-tax Act, 1961. Governs the maximum ('specified') number of tax audit assignments a member may sign in a financial year under Chapter VI of the Council General Guidelines, 2008.
topics: specified number of tax audit assignments
seedText: This ICAI clarification addresses the 'specified number of tax audit assignments' under Chapter VI of the Council General Guidelines, 2008, which caps the number of tax audits under Section 44AB of the Income-tax Act, 1961 that a member in practice may accept and sign in a financial year. The limit was originally 45 assignments per member. The Council, at its 331st meeting held from 10th to 12th February 2014, decided to increase the specified number of tax audit assignments for a practising Chartered Accountant, whether as an individual or as a partner in a firm, from 45 to 60. This enhanced limit of 60 became effective for audits conducted during the financial year 2014-15 and onwards. In the case of a firm of Chartered Accountants in practice, the specified number of tax audit assignments is computed per partner of the firm; the clarification illustrates that a firm with 10 partners can collectively sign the resulting multiple of tax audit reports (e.g. at 45 per partner, 450 reports). Members are also required to comply with the Standard on Quality Control (SQC) 1 in respect of these assignments.

verificationNote: Fetched the exact canonicalUrl on www.icai.org (allowed host). seedText: This Income Tax Department e-filing help page ('TDS Compliance') addresses deductor obligations and the transition from the Income-tax Act, 1961 to the new Income-tax Act, 2025, which takes effect from 1 April 2026. The governing rule stated is that the Act applicable to a TDS transaction depends on the 'earlier of the event of credit or payment': where that event occurs on or before 31 March 2026 the 1961 Act applies, and from 1 April 2026 onward the 2025 Act applies. The page lists the challan-cum-statement forms used for specified deductions under the 1961 Act - Form 26QB (TDS on transfer of immovable property, section 194-IA), Form 26QC (TDS on rent by individuals/HUF, section 194-IB), Form 26QD (TDS on contractual/professional payments by individuals/HUF, section 194M) and Form 26QE (TDS on transfer of virtual digital assets, section 194S) - and references a new unified form under the 2025 Act. It confirms that the Return Preparation Utility (RPU) and the TRACES portal support statements under both the old and new frameworks during the transition. The page is organised as a set of FAQs covering ongoing contracts, preservation of TDS rates, correction of erroneous section citations, and payment/credit timing scenarios. publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India (e-Filing portal)
title: Annual Information Statement (AIS) - e-Filing Help
applicability: Taxpayers and CAs reconciling TDS/TCS, SFT and tax-payment data before filing the return; explains AIS Part A/Part B, feedback, TIS, and how AIS differs from Form 26AS.
seedText: The Annual Information Statement (AIS) help page describes AIS as a comprehensive view of information for a taxpayer, whose objectives are to display complete information before filing the return, promote voluntary compliance, enable seamless prefilling of the return, and deter non-compliance. AIS is presented in two parts. Part A (General Information) shows PAN, masked Aadhaar number, name, date of birth/incorporation/formation, mobile number, email and address. Part B carries the financial information - TDS/TCS entries (with information code, description and value), Statement of Financial Transactions (SFT), tax payments such as advance tax and self-assessment tax, demand and refund, and other information such as salary annexure, interest on refund and foreign remittances. For each item AIS shows both the reported value and the modified value after taxpayer feedback is considered. Taxpayers may submit online feedback on each displayed transaction and receive an acknowledgement; an AIS Consolidated Feedback file summarises non-confirmatory feedback. A Taxpayer Information Summary (TIS) aggregates the information category-wise and feeds prefilling. AIS can be downloaded in PDF, JSON and CSV formats; the PDF is password protected using PAN in lower case followed by date of birth/incorporation in DDMMYYYY. Access is via login at incometax.gov.in, then the 'Annual Information Statement (AIS)' menu on the dashboard, or e-File > Income Tax Return > View AIS. The page notes the key difference from Form 26AS: Form 26AS on TRACES shows primarily TDS/TCS and tax-payment data, whereas AIS provides a wider set of information plus a feedback mechanism.

title: View Tax Credit Mismatch FAQs - Form 26AS reconciliation
applicability: Taxpayers/CAs whose TDS or tax-payment credit claimed in the ITR does not match Form 26AS; explains what 26AS contains and how to resolve challan/PAN and TDS-statement mismatches.
seedText: This 'View Tax Credit Mismatch' FAQ on the e-filing portal explains Form 26AS and how to reconcile tax credits. It defines Form 26AS as a consolidated Annual Information Statement for a particular Financial Year, and states that it reflects details of TDS, TCS, advance tax and self-assessment tax deposited, refunds, and specified financial transactions, along with demand and refund information. A central point is that the tax credit a taxpayer may claim in the income-tax return is restricted to the amount reflected in Form 26AS; where the credit claimed in the ITR exceeds what appears in 26AS, a mismatch arises. The FAQ guides taxpayers to validate challan identification particulars (such as BSR code, challan serial number, date and amount) and the PAN quoted, since an incorrect PAN or wrong challan details are common reasons a deposit does not appear against the taxpayer. For TDS mismatches, it directs the taxpayer to follow up with the deductor so the deductor files or corrects the quarterly TDS statement and the credit is reflected correctly. The FAQ set covers: what Form 26AS is; why self-assessment or advance tax paid may not appear in the statement; how to identify a tax credit mismatch and the messages shown on comparison; and how to resolve a mismatch in an already-filed return depending on whether the underlying issue is a TDS credit or another type of credit.

publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India (e-Filing portal)
title: TDS on Cash Withdrawal under Section 194N - FAQs
applicability: Banks, co-operative banks and post offices deducting TDS on cash withdrawals, and account holders (including non-filers) crossing the ₹20 lakh / ₹1 crore cash-withdrawal thresholds under section 194N.
seedText: This FAQ page covers TDS on cash withdrawals under section 194N of the Income-tax Act, 1961, applicable from 1 September 2019 (FY 2019-20). It explains that banks (private, public and co-operative) and post offices must deduct TDS when cash is paid from a person's account(s) beyond prescribed limits in a financial year. Two threshold regimes apply. Where the person has filed returns of income for all or any of the three preceding assessment years, TDS at 2% applies on the aggregate cash withdrawn exceeding ₹1 crore in the financial year. Where the person has not filed returns of income for any of the three preceding assessment years, TDS applies at 2% on the amount exceeding ₹20 lakh and at 5% on the amount exceeding ₹1 crore. The FAQ lists persons and entities excluded from section 194N, including the Government, banks, co-operative societies engaged in the business of banking, post offices, business correspondents of a banking company, white-label ATM operators, and other persons notified by the Central Government (for example certain commission agents/traders operating under an APMC and authorised dealers/money changers). It clarifies that the deductor is the bank or post office maintaining the account, and that the withdrawal limits are computed with reference to the aggregate cash withdrawn from all the accounts a person holds with that payer.
